method: grep for Platform.OS across services/ and hooks/useKScan.js in the traced capture->upload path, plus direct read of hooks/useKScan.js and services/privacyImageUpload.ts
summary: No Platform.OS branch was found anywhere in the traced capture -> preprocess -> upload path (hooks/useKScan.js capturePhoto/selectGalleryPhoto, services/privacyImageUpload.ts, services/scanIdentification.ts). Both platforms run through the same Expo cross-platform APIs (expo-camera CameraView, expo-image-picker, expo-image-manipulator) with the same numeric parameters. iOS and Android therefore receive byte-for-byte-equivalent JS-level preprocessing instructions. This is proven from source, not assumed.

ios.captureApi: expo-camera CameraView.takePictureAsync({ quality: 0.7 }) [camera] or expo-image-picker launchImageLibraryAsync({ mediaTypes: ['images'], quality: 1, allowsEditing: false, allowsMultipleSelection: false }) [gallery]
ios.imageFormat: JPEG (expo-camera default output; re-encoded to JPEG explicitly at the privacy-preprocessing stage)
ios.orientationHandling: NOT_FOUND (no explicit orientation-correction call observed in the traced path; expo-image-manipulator applies EXIF orientation during resize per its own documented behavior, but this repository does not add extra orientation logic)
ios.exifHandling: not explicitly requested or stripped by name; EXIF metadata is dropped as a side effect of re-encoding through ImageManipulator.manipulateAsync (a fresh JPEG derivative carries no source EXIF block)
ios.metadataStripping: confirmed via services/privacyImageUpload.ts honestPolicy() -> metadataStripped:true after the manipulateAsync re-encode
ios.cropping: none in the traced path (allowsEditing:false on gallery picker; no crop transform passed to manipulateAsync)
ios.rotation: NOT_FOUND (no explicit rotate transform passed to manipulateAsync in the traced calls)
ios.platformOSBranches: NONE FOUND in hooks/useKScan.js, services/privacyImageUpload.ts, services/scanIdentification.ts
ios.nativeModuleDifferences: NOT_PROVEN from JS source alone. expo-camera and expo-image-manipulator wrap AVFoundation (iOS) vs Camera2/CameraX (Android) natively; any pixel-level difference in JPEG encoder behavior between the two native stacks is outside what static JS-source tracing can prove. Documented as a boundary of this discovery pass, not as 'no difference exists'.
ios.uploadEncoding: data:image/jpeg;base64,<...> string sent as imageBase64 in the scan-identify POST body

android.captureApi: identical call sites to iOS - expo-camera CameraView.takePictureAsync({ quality: 0.7 }) [camera] or expo-image-picker launchImageLibraryAsync({ mediaTypes: ['images'], quality: 1, allowsEditing: false, allowsMultipleSelection: false }) [gallery]
android.resizeDimensionsAnalysisPass: width 896px, quality 0.75, base64 true (identical to iOS)
android.orientationHandling: NOT_FOUND (same code path as iOS - no Android-specific branch)
android.exifHandling: same re-encode-strips-EXIF behavior as iOS; no Android-specific EXIF logic found
android.cropping: none in the traced path (same code path as iOS)
android.nativeModuleDifferences: NOT_PROVEN from JS source alone, same caveat as iOS - Camera2/CameraX vs AVFoundation encoder behavior is not visible to static JS tracing.

platformDifferences: NONE PROVEN AT THE JS/PARAMETER LEVEL. The capture quality, resize dimensions, compression quality, format, and upload encoding are identical constants shared by both platforms through Expo's cross-platform camera/image APIs. Any real-world quality difference between an iOS and an Android capture of the same garment would originate below the JS layer (native camera sensor/ISP behavior, native JPEG encoder, on-device HDR/portrait processing before the frame ever reaches takePictureAsync) - none of which is visible to source-code tracing and none of which this build fabricates evidence for.
captureCeilingNote: Per spec section 11/12: this build implements capture-profile IDENTIFIERS and a deterministic, descriptor-level degradation transform (captureProfiles/profiles.js) that encodes the REAL resize/quality constants above so fixtures can be tagged and stratified by profile. It does NOT build a native-image emulator and does NOT fabricate paired iOS/Android photographs; real pixel-level parity evidence requires an owner-supplied paired corpus (see FINAL REPORT 'RECOMMENDED REAL CORPUS').
